correctness.rationale: Four-round equivalence follows by matching first sides, then the five pair positions, then the set of atomic fourth-extensions. Checked directly from the group axioms: a positive extension adjacent to a unique specified distinct vertex has q candidates and at most two exclusions (a common neighbor with another same-side selection, or the opposite-side selected vertex itself). Two required neighbors are either impossible or determine a unique candidate. Its freshness and incidence with the third selection are fixed by the listed pair/triple position, including concurrence and the groups of the three selections. Zero-neighbor extensions always exist uncolored for q≥3; on a prescribed side q≥4, with k opposite-side distinct selections the excluded count is at most kq+(3−k). For q=3 the only possible side-specific obstruction is k=3, and then the three neighborhoods cover exactly when disjoint, i.e. the three selections exhaust one group. Each raw third-position is realized for q≥3: new-group concurrence with an intersecting pair uses one point per unused group, and new-group nonconcurrence uses q−1 per unused group. In an incident mixed pair, in the old group all other points are off-line; in a nonincident mixed pair the off-line positions in the old group number q−2, and dually for old-group lines missing the point. The other incidences are available from the matching/group counts. This fixes all triple extensions uniformly in the stated ranges, including named order 3 versus order 3 with the same extra obstruction; no orbit-transitivity premise is needed. I also calculated the five raw uncolored profile counts for field orders 3 and 5 independently and obtained (4,6,10,7,9) in both; these finite spot checks are not the general proof. At q=2 the net graph is connected (different groups on one side have a common neighbor, linking also same-group vertices through a different group) and 2-regular, hence C8 with its bipartition, unique even with side names. The rank-four degree test singles out q=2 and the named three-point line-cover sentence singles out q=3 among q≥3. The smallest net orders in the top classes are 3 and 4, as realized by finite-field nets, so 18 and 32 are sharp only within the family.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Projective-plane incidence has common neighbors for every distinct same-side pair; the deleted-class net has parallel groups and lacks those common neighbors. Generalized quadrangles have their own incidence axiom, including unique connection from a nonincident point to a line; a net has q−1 such connecting lines, not generally one. These are not encompassing results for the net.
